Dana Whitfield, category manager. I do not think we have met. So, what does your company do?
Fernando da Cunha. We are a group of companies in Brazil, and four of them make point-of-sale material — the price tags and the shelf labels you read in the aisle.
Right. And who do you work with down there?
We supply forty-seven of the fifty largest supermarket chains in the country, and eight of the ten largest drugstore chains. We have been working with most of them for over a decade.
That is a serious list. Do you make it yourselves, or do you buy it in?
We make it. We have two manufacturing plants, and the design is in-house as well. We only source the raw material abroad.
Then the question everybody here is going to ask you. What is your lead time?

Fifteen days from the order, and that is the reason the big chains stay with us. In a group this size you wear several hats, so I sign the contract and I also answer for the delivery. And you — how many stores are you buying for?
We are a group of companies, and four of them make point-of-sale material.
We make it ourselves, and our lead time is fifteen days.
And you, how long have you been buying for this chain?

All right, my turn. We make shelf labels and price tags, which is the boring half of the store and also the half everybody actually looks at. We are in four thousand stores across eleven states, and I say that first because it is the only thing a buyer can do anything with. We have been doing this for thirty-one years. My father started it in a garage with one printing press, and I would love to tell you that I had a plan when I took over, but I did not. What I had was a customer who needed forty thousand labels in nine days. The mistake I see at every one of these fairs is people opening with the price. The price is the fourth question. Nobody in thirty-one years has ever bought from me because of the first number I said.

People ask what we listen for in the first two minutes, and the honest answer is that we listen for a reference point. Most suppliers describe the product. They tell me the thickness of the paper, the finish, the machine it came off, and none of that means anything to me yet, because I have nothing to compare it to. A good opening is three things. Who you already supply, how fast you deliver, and one thing you have changed in the last year. That last one matters more than people think, because it is the only part that tells me what you will be like to work with when something goes wrong. And before somebody asks, no, imperfect English has never cost anybody a contract with us. A slow, clear answer is worth more than a fast one I have to guess at. We can look the price up later. We cannot look up whether you are going to answer the phone in February.

A large supermarket changes something like forty thousand paper labels in a single week, and that figure is quoted so often that people stop hearing what it hides, which is the number of staff hours behind it. That is where the cost actually sits, and not in the paper. Electronic shelf labels were supposed to end all of that a decade ago, and the change has been far slower than anybody predicted. The screens turned out to be the cheap part. Fitting them along every aisle of a chain with six hundred stores takes years, and most chains have been running the two systems side by side for far longer than they planned. We spoke to half a dozen printing suppliers for this series. Almost none of them are trying to compete on the shelf edge any more. They have moved into promotional signage, the material that changes every week and is still printed, and several of them told us the same thing. The shelf label was never the business. The deadline was.
